claims.claim: ∼17 nm filaments on the membrane in intercellular bridges before cytokinesis disappear when CHMP2A is missing.
claims.source: Finally, ∼17 nm filaments on the membrane in intercellular bridges before cytokinesis disappear when CHMP2A is missing, suggesting that they too might represent a form of ESCRT-III polymer (Guizetti et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Depleting Vps4A & B by RNAi caused ESCRT-III proteins to redistribute onto puncta localized throughout the cell.
claims.source: Depleting Vps4A & B, the two Vps4 proteins present in human cells, by RNAi (Figure 1B) caused ESCRT-III proteins to redistribute onto puncta localized throughout the cell (Figure 1A, middle panels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: A significant fraction of ESCRT-III proteins accumulated in the detergent insoluble fraction characteristic of polymerized ESCRT-III after depleting Vps4A & B.
claims.source: Sedimentation of detergent solubilized cell extracts further demonstrated that a significant fraction of ESCRT-III proteins accumulated in the detergent insoluble fraction characteristic of polymerized ESCRT-III (Figure 1C; Shim et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Deep-etch EM of plasma membranes from cultured cells depleted of Vps4A & B revealed unique filamentous assemblies.
claims.source: Deep-etch EM of plasma membranes from cultured cells depleted of Vps4A & B revealed unique filamentous assemblies intermingled among otherwise typical cytoskeletal structures, clathrin lattices, and caveolae (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Gold particles marking CHMP6, CHMP2B, and CHMP1B bound on or near filaments and filament spirals but not elsewhere on membranes from cells depleted of Vps4A & B.
claims.source: Because these filaments resemble previously described ESCRT-III polymers, we used antibodies recognizing several ESCRT-III proteins and found that gold particles marking each of the proteins examined (CHMP6, CHMP2B, and CHMP1B) bound on or near filaments and filament spirals but not elsewhere on membranes from cells depleted of Vps4A & B (Figure 2B) or on membranes from control HeLa cells (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The overall diameter of the spiral assemblies was 108 ± 30 nm.
claims.source: The overall diameter of the spiral assemblies was 108 ± 30 nm (Figure 3C), with an average of four 360° turns in each spiral.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III spirals have an average of four 360° turns in each spiral.
claims.source: The overall diameter of the spiral assemblies was 108 ± 30 nm (Figure 3C), with an average of four 360° turns in each spiral.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: The total length of the filament in each spiral was 660 ± 350 nm.
claims.source: The total length of the filament in each spiral was 660 ± 350 nm.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III spirals surround and cover an area of membrane that corresponds well with that needed to generate a vesicle ∼50 nm in diameter—the typical size of ILVs in mammalian cells.
claims.source: Interestingly, ESCRT-III spirals surround and cover an area of membrane that corresponds well with that needed to generate a vesicle ∼50 nm in diameter—the typical size of ILVs in mammalian cells (Murk et al., 2003)—suggesting that an initial ESCRT-III circle might define the content of an incipient vesicle.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements and comparison to known ILV sizes from cited literature.

claims.claim: Both left- and right-handed spirals were found even in the same field of view.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found both left- and right-handed spirals even in the same field of view (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observations in deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The apparent diameter of the finest filaments in ESCRT-III spirals was ∼4 nm.
claims.source: The apparent diameter of the finest filaments in ESCRT-III spirals was ∼4 nm (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Filament width varied from 4 to as much as 15 nm in both conical and flat spirals.
claims.source: Filament width varied from 4 to as much as 15 nm in both conical and flat spirals (Figure 3D), excluding differences in accessibility to platinum deposition as a primary cause of the differences.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Overexpressed FLAG-tagged CHMP4 proteins create extensive networks of interconnected curved but flat filaments.
claims.source: We previously found that overexpressed FLAG-tagged CHMP4 proteins create extensive networks of interconnected curved but flat filaments (Hanson et al., 2008) and others have seen that CHMP4B and yeast Snf7 behave similarly in vitro (Pires et al., 2009; Henne et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claims.claim: Untagged CHMP4A filaments circle and spiral along the membrane to form an anastomosing network but do not couple this to changes in membrane shape.
claims.source: As before, CHMP4A filaments circle and spiral along the membrane to form an anastomosing network but do not couple this to changes in membrane shape (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Membranes from cells co-expressing 'open' CHMP4A(α1–α5) and full-length CHMP2A were studded with eversions lined by spiraling filaments.
claims.source: Strikingly, membranes from cells co-expressing 'open' CHMP4A(α1–α5) and full-length CHMP2A were studded with eversions lined by spiraling filaments (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Similar membrane-deforming filaments developed when full-length CHMP4A was coexpressed with 'open' CHMP2A(α1–α5).
claims.source: Similar membrane-deforming filaments developed when we coexpressed full-length CHMP4A with 'open' CHMP2A(α1–α5) (not shown), demonstrating that the shape changes do not depend on C-terminal autoinhibitory sequences in either protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: The shape changes in ESCRT-III filaments do not depend on C-terminal autoinhibitory sequences in either CHMP4A or CHMP2A.
claims.source: Similar membrane-deforming filaments developed when we coexpressed full-length CHMP4A with 'open' CHMP2A(α1–α5) (not shown), demonstrating that the shape changes do not depend on C-terminal autoinhibitory sequences in either protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both combinations of full-length and truncated proteins produce similar results.

claims.claim: HEK293T cells transiently expressing HIV-1 Gag produce abundant VLPs.
claims.source: HEK293T cells transiently expressing HIV-1 Gag (Figure 5) or Gag-GFP (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) produce abundant VLPs that are readily apparent by deep-etch EM both on and around cells as well as beneath unroofed plasma membranes (Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Expressing a dominant negative mutant of Vps4A (Vps4A E228Q) or silencing Vps4 increased the amount of Gag-GFP or Gag on the plasma membrane.
claims.source: As expected, expressing a dominant negative mutant of Vps4A (Vps4A E228Q) or silencing Vps4 as above increased the amount of Gag-GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) or Gag (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) on the plasma membrane and decreased release of VLPs as detected by particle analysis methods (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy and deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Expressing a dominant negative mutant of Vps4A (Vps4A E228Q) or silencing Vps4 decreased release of VLPs.
claims.source: As expected, expressing a dominant negative mutant of Vps4A (Vps4A E228Q) or silencing Vps4 as above increased the amount of Gag-GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) or Gag (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) on the plasma membrane and decreased release of VLPs as detected by particle analysis methods (data not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by particle analysis methods mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: In cells lacking Vps4, Gag assemblies on the plasma membrane were often surrounded by a single filament not seen in control cells.
claims.source: Strikingly, in cells lacking Vps4 Gag assemblies on the plasma membrane were now often surrounded by a single filament not seen in control cells (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The encircling filaments around Gag assemblies ranged from 4.5–12.8 nm (average 8.6 ± 1.6 nm, n = 96) in width.
claims.source: The encircling filaments appeared similar to the ESCRT-III filaments examined above, each ranging from 4.5–12.8 nm (average 8.6 ± 1.6 nm, n = 96) in width with the majority wide enough to contain more than one ∼4 nm substrand.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: Immunolabeling confirmed that ESCRT-III proteins localized to the perimeter of Gag assemblies coincident with the filaments.
claims.source: Immunolabeling confirmed that ESCRT-III proteins localized to the perimeter of Gag assemblies coincident with the filaments (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunogold labeling data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The encircling filaments surrounded Gag assemblies of various sizes ranging from ∼60–150 nm.
claims.source: Interestingly, the encircling filaments surrounded Gag assemblies of various sizes ranging from ∼60–150 nm suggesting that the threshold amount of Gag needed to activate ESCRT-III assembly may be decreased in the setting of reduced Vps4 leading to premature nucleation of the ESCRT-III ring.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III filaments were frequently connected to the central Gag assembly by perpendicular 'struts' ∼14 nm long.
claims.source: We noticed that ESCRT-III filaments (in cells depleted of Vps4) were frequently connected to the central Gag assembly by perpendicular 'struts' ∼14 nm long (Figure 6, see green highlighting in inset).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The C-terminal p6 domain of Gag contains a PTAP motif essential for interaction with the ESCRT-I protein Tsg101.
claims.source: The C-terminal p6 domain of Gag contains a PTAP motif (essential for interaction with the ESCRT-I protein Tsg101 [Garrus et al., 2001]) and a LYPXnL motif (involved in interaction with ALIX [Strack et al., 2003]) and has been shown to be essential for budding of Gag VLPs as well as HIV-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The C-terminal p6 domain of Gag contains a LYPXnL motif involved in interaction with ALIX.
claims.source: The C-terminal p6 domain of Gag contains a PTAP motif (essential for interaction with the ESCRT-I protein Tsg101 [Garrus et al., 2001]) and a LYPXnL motif (involved in interaction with ALIX [Strack et al., 2003]) and has been shown to be essential for budding of Gag VLPs as well as HIV-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: The p6 domain has been shown to be essential for budding of Gag VLPs as well as HIV-1.
claims.source: The C-terminal p6 domain of Gag contains a PTAP motif (essential for interaction with the ESCRT-I protein Tsg101 [Garrus et al., 2001]) and a LYPXnL motif (involved in interaction with ALIX [Strack et al., 2003]) and has been shown to be essential for budding of Gag VLPs as well as HIV-1.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: In cells expressing GagΔp6, very few VLPs were released and instead large numbers of arrested Gag-containing buds accumulated on the surface.
claims.source: In cells expressing GagΔp6, very few VLPs were released and instead large numbers of arrested Gag-containing buds accumulated on the surface (Figure 7 and not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The p6 domain is required for VLP release.
claims.source: Importantly, this was true regardless of whether Vps4 was present or not, confirming that the p6 domain is required for VLP release.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GagΔp6 fails to release VLPs in both conditions.

claims.claim: p6 sequences are required to recruit ESCRT-III.
claims.source: On unroofed plasma membranes Gag assemblies similar to those formed by full-length Gag were observed but were not surrounded by ESCRT-III rings (Figure 7), demonstrating that p6 sequences are required to recruit ESCRT-III.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations showing absence of ESCRT-III rings around GagΔp6 assemblies in Figure 7.

claims.claim: A first role for ESCRT-III is to encircle and thereby delineate cargo and membrane destined for inclusion in a vesicle or VLP.
claims.source: In this model, a first role for ESCRT-III is to encircle and thereby delineate cargo and membrane destined for inclusion in a vesicle or VLP (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed structures.

claims.claim: An important and previously unappreciated role for Vps4 is to release connection(s) between the ESCRT-III filament and cargo.
claims.source: Because encircled Gag assemblies uniquely accumulate when Vps4 is missing (Figure 6), we propose that an important and previously unappreciated role for Vps4 is to release connection(s) between the ESCRT-III filament and cargo, perhaps displacing the struts while also opening the ring.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observation that encircled Gag assemblies accumulate when Vps4 is depleted.

claims.claim: The ESCRT-III filament can grow to adopt its preferred shape as a conical spiral potentially driving neck constriction and vesicle release.
claims.source: The ESCRT-III filament can then grow to adopt its preferred shape as a conical spiral (Figure 8B) potentially driving neck constriction and vesicle release as shown (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on interpolation between observed structures.

claims.claim: Vps4 is responsible for disassembling ESCRT-III filaments to recycle their subunits during or after vesicle release.
claims.source: Finally (and not shown), Vps4 is also responsible for disassembling ESCRT-III filaments to recycle their subunits during or after vesicle release.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Fluorescently tagged Vps4 is recruited to growing viral particles before they are released.
claims.source: Fluorescently tagged Vps4 is recruited to growing viral particles before they are released (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011), Vps4 appears at two stages prior to cellular abscission (Elia et al., 2011), ESCRT-III and Vps4 are recruited simultaneously to the centroid of dividing Crenarchaea (Samson et al., 2011), and perturbing Vps4 function and/or regulation changes ILV size and/or release in yeast (Nickerson et al., 2010; Wemmer et al., 2011; Adell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Vps4 appears at two stages prior to cellular abscission.
claims.source: Fluorescently tagged Vps4 is recruited to growing viral particles before they are released (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011), Vps4 appears at two stages prior to cellular abscission (Elia et al., 2011), ESCRT-III and Vps4 are recruited simultaneously to the centroid of dividing Crenarchaea (Samson et al., 2011), and perturbing Vps4 function and/or regulation changes ILV size and/or release in yeast (Nickerson et al., 2010; Wemmer et al., 2011; Adell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III and Vps4 are recruited simultaneously to the centroid of dividing Crenarchaea.
claims.source: Fluorescently tagged Vps4 is recruited to growing viral particles before they are released (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011), Vps4 appears at two stages prior to cellular abscission (Elia et al., 2011), ESCRT-III and Vps4 are recruited simultaneously to the centroid of dividing Crenarchaea (Samson et al., 2011), and perturbing Vps4 function and/or regulation changes ILV size and/or release in yeast (Nickerson et al., 2010; Wemmer et al., 2011; Adell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Perturbing Vps4 function and/or regulation changes ILV size and/or release in yeast.
claims.source: Fluorescently tagged Vps4 is recruited to growing viral particles before they are released (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011), Vps4 appears at two stages prior to cellular abscission (Elia et al., 2011), ESCRT-III and Vps4 are recruited simultaneously to the centroid of dividing Crenarchaea (Samson et al., 2011), and perturbing Vps4 function and/or regulation changes ILV size and/or release in yeast (Nickerson et al., 2010; Wemmer et al., 2011; Adell et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Interfering with Vps4 activity will trap ESCRT-III around the base of incipient vesicular structures.
claims.source: A prediction of our model is that interfering with Vps4 activity—whether by depleting it or expressing a dominant negative mutant—will trap ESCRT-III around the base of incipient vesicular structures and in particular around the base of emerging Gag assemblies.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claims.claim: Trapped ESCRT-III will remain attached to Gag inside any VLPs that are ultimately released when Vps4 activity is interfered with.
claims.source: This trapped ESCRT-III will remain attached to Gag inside any VLPs that are ultimately released.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claims.claim: Interfering with Vps4 activity will increase ESCRT-III recovered in whatever VLPs are released.
claims.source: This in turn will increase ESCRT-III recovered in whatever VLPs are released, something that we (data not shown) and others (Van Engelenburg et al., 2014) have in fact observed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations by the authors and cited research.

claims.claim: Endogenous ESCRT-III proteins including CHMP4A and CHMP2B are diffusely localized in cells with little steady-state concentration on endosomes.
claims.source: Endogenous ESCRT-III proteins including CHMP4A and CHMP2B are diffusely localized in cells with little steady-state concentration on endosomes despite their known role in lumenal vesicle formation (Figure 1A, left panels).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III proteins and Vps4 are present for a few minutes or less at their site of action during viral particle release.
claims.source: This is not surprising given measurements in live cells showing that both they and Vps4 are present for a few minutes or less at their site of action during viral particle release (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011) or cytokinetic abscission (Elia et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to live cell imaging studies.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III proteins and Vps4 are present for a few minutes or less at their site of action during cytokinetic abscission.
claims.source: This is not surprising given measurements in live cells showing that both they and Vps4 are present for a few minutes or less at their site of action during viral particle release (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011) or cytokinetic abscission (Elia et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to live cell imaging studies.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III puncta could reflect a role for ESCRT-III in creating outwardly-directed vesicles known as ectosomes that bud from the plasma membrane.
claims.source: Their presence could reflect a role for ESCRT-III in creating outwardly-directed vesicles known as ectosomes that bud from the plasma membrane (Stein and Luzio, 1991; Nabhan et al., 2012; Choudhuri et al., 2014; Jimenez et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed ESCRT-III puncta on the plasma membrane, supported by citations.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III puncta could be transferred to the plasma membrane by MVB exocytosis.
claims.source: Alternatively, ESCRT-III puncta could be transferred to the plasma membrane by MVB exocytosis (Thery, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed ESCRT-III puncta on the plasma membrane, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Similar filament spirals were seen in siRNA treated HEK293T, U2OS, and MCF-7 cells.
claims.source: Similar filament spirals were seen in siRNA treated HEK293T, U2OS, and MCF-7 cells (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations mentioned in the figure legend.

claims.claim: The shape of the spirals on the membrane varied, ranging from clearly conical to flat.
claims.source: The shape of the spirals on the membrane varied, ranging from clearly conical to flat.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observations in deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: 61% of spirals were conical (108 ± 29 nm) and 39% were flat (102 ± 20 nm).
claims.source: (C) Outer diameter of spirals defined as conical or flat based on appearance in 3D (n = 184, 61% conical 108 ± 29 nm; 39% flat 102 ± 20 nm).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Wider filaments were most prevalent at the perimeter while thin filaments occurred throughout but were almost always present near the spirals' center.
claims.source: Wider filaments—sometimes with a split down their middle suggesting the presence of parallel substrands—were most prevalent at the perimeter while thin filaments occurred throughout but were almost always present near the spirals' center.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observations in deep-etch EM images.

claims.claim: Filaments sometimes abruptly changed width.
claims.source: Filaments sometimes abruptly changed width (see examples highlighted in Figure 3A) further supporting the presence of subfilaments within wider structures.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observations in deep-etch EM images shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: ESCRT-II has two ESCRT-III nucleating sites.
claims.source: Given the functional requirement for two ESCRT-III nucleating sites in ESCRT-II (Teis et al., 2010) or Alix (Pires et al., 2009), one possibility is that parallel filaments create the outer turns of a spiral but give way to single filaments with the potential for tighter curvature near the spiral's center.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Alix has two ESCRT-III nucleating sites.
claims.source: Given the functional requirement for two ESCRT-III nucleating sites in ESCRT-II (Teis et al., 2010) or Alix (Pires et al., 2009), one possibility is that parallel filaments create the outer turns of a spiral but give way to single filaments with the potential for tighter curvature near the spiral's center.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: CHMP4A filaments remain flat when built from a constitutively 'open' CHMP4(α1–α5) truncation mutant.
claims.source: CHMP4A filaments also remain flat when built from a constitutively 'open' CHMP4(α1–α5) truncation mutant (Shim et al., 2007; Figure 4B) or a K52E mutant that enhances Snf7 assembly in yeast (Henne et al., 2012) (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: CHMP4A filaments remain flat when built from a K52E mutant that enhances Snf7 assembly in yeast.
claims.source: CHMP4A filaments also remain flat when built from a constitutively 'open' CHMP4(α1–α5) truncation mutant (Shim et al., 2007; Figure 4B) or a K52E mutant that enhances Snf7 assembly in yeast (Henne et al., 2012) (not shown).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claims.claim: Full-length CHMP4A and CHMP2A do not efficiently coassemble.
claims.source: Previous biochemical analyses showed that full-length CHMP4A and CHMP2A do not efficiently coassemble while heteropolymers form readily when either protein is activated by deleting its autoinhibitory domain (Shim et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior biochemical research by the authors.

claims.claim: Heteropolymers of CHMP4A and CHMP2A form readily when either protein is activated by deleting its autoinhibitory domain.
claims.source: Previous biochemical analyses showed that full-length CHMP4A and CHMP2A do not efficiently coassemble while heteropolymers form readily when either protein is activated by deleting its autoinhibitory domain (Shim et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior biochemical research by the authors.

claims.claim: Subunits such as CHMP2A coassemble with CHMP4 to change the structure of the filament and its effects on membrane shape.
claims.source: The fact that ESCRT-III heteropolymers differ from the sum of their parts supports a model in which subunits such as CHMP2A coassemble with CHMP4 to change the structure of the filament and its effects on membrane shape.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that coexpression produces different structures than either protein alone.

claims.claim: Similar changes in filament morphology were previously seen with purified proteins in vitro.
claims.source: Similar changes in filament morphology were previously seen with purified proteins in vitro (Henne et al., 2012) suggesting that distinctive heteropolymer shape may be a general feature of ESCRT-III biology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior in vitro research.

claims.claim: HIV-1 assembly is driven by polymerization of the virally encoded Gag polyprotein.
claims.source: HIV-1 assembly is driven by polymerization of the virally encoded Gag polyprotein, which recruits cellular ESCRT proteins to facilitate virion release from the plasma membrane and can be expressed alone to produce virus-like particles (VLPs) (Gheysen et al., 1989; Karacostas et al., 1989; Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Gag recruits cellular ESCRT proteins to facilitate virion release from the plasma membrane.
claims.source: HIV-1 assembly is driven by polymerization of the virally encoded Gag polyprotein, which recruits cellular ESCRT proteins to facilitate virion release from the plasma membrane and can be expressed alone to produce virus-like particles (VLPs) (Gheysen et al., 1989; Karacostas et al., 1989; Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Gag can be expressed alone to produce virus-like particles (VLPs).
claims.source: HIV-1 assembly is driven by polymerization of the virally encoded Gag polyprotein, which recruits cellular ESCRT proteins to facilitate virion release from the plasma membrane and can be expressed alone to produce virus-like particles (VLPs) (Gheysen et al., 1989; Karacostas et al., 1989; Sundquist and Krausslich, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: ESCRTs and especially ESCRT-III play important roles both in completing the viral sphere and in severing its connection to the cell.
claims.source: Current thinking based on electron tomography of immature virions (Wright et al., 2007; Carlson et al., 2008; Briggs et al., 2009) and bud sites (Carlson et al., 2008) is that ESCRTs and especially ESCRT-III play important roles both in completing the viral sphere (that is only 2/3 covered by polymerized Gag) and in severing its connection to the cell.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electron tomography studies.

claims.claim: The viral sphere is only 2/3 covered by polymerized Gag.
claims.source: Current thinking based on electron tomography of immature virions (Wright et al., 2007; Carlson et al., 2008; Briggs et al., 2009) and bud sites (Carlson et al., 2008) is that ESCRTs and especially ESCRT-III play important roles both in completing the viral sphere (that is only 2/3 covered by polymerized Gag) and in severing its connection to the cell.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electron tomography studies.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III and Vps4 are transiently recruited to Gag assemblies to mediate release.
claims.source: ESCRT-III and Vps4 are transiently recruited to Gag assemblies to mediate release (Jouvenet et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Gag-GFP assemblies were less uniform in size and shape than those containing Gag.
claims.source: By deep-etch EM, Gag-GFP assemblies were less uniform in size and shape than those containing Gag (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), consistent with the irregular distribution of Gag-GFP seen by thin section EM (Pornillos et al., 2003) and with the decreased Gag content of VLPs containing Gag fused to similarly sized fluorescent proteins (Gunzenhauser et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by deep-etch EM observations and citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There was no evidence to indicate the presence of ESCRT-III on or near Gag assemblies in cells with normal Vps4 levels.
claims.source: Notably there was no evidence by direct viewing or immunolabeling (not shown) to indicate the presence of ESCRT-III on or near any of these Gag assemblies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of observed ESCRT-III in the experimental conditions.

claims.claim: ESCRT-III is only transiently recruited after Gag assembly is essentially complete.
claims.source: This is not surprising given live cell studies showing that ESCRT-III and Vps4 are only transiently recruited after Gag assembly is essentially complete (Baumgartel et al., 2011; Jouvenet et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to live cell imaging studies.

claims.claim: The struts resemble previous negative stain images of purified Alix bound perpendicularly to Snf7 filaments.
claims.source: These struts resemble previous negative stain images of purified Alix bound perpendicularly to Snf7 filaments (Pires et al., 2009) although based on size they could also correspond to ESCRT-I (Boura et al., 2011), an ESCRT-I-ESCRT-II supercomplex (Boura et al., 2012), or something else altogether.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to prior structural studies, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Based on size, the struts could correspond to ESCRT-I.
claims.source: These struts resemble previous negative stain images of purified Alix bound perpendicularly to Snf7 filaments (Pires et al., 2009) although based on size they could also correspond to ESCRT-I (Boura et al., 2011), an ESCRT-I-ESCRT-II supercomplex (Boura et al., 2012), or something else altogether.

results.result: Depleting Vps4A and Vps4B in mammalian cells causes ESCRT-III proteins to redistribute from diffuse cytoplasmic localization to puncta throughout the cell and accumulate in detergent-insoluble fractions characteristic of polymerized ESCRT-III.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C25, C65, and C99 are supported by immunofluorescence microscopy (Figure 1A), immunoblotting (Figure 1B), and sedimentation assays (Figure 1C). The data demonstrate that RNAi-mediated depletion of both Vps4 proteins stabilizes ESCRT-III polymers on membranes, consistent with Vps4's known role in ESCRT-III disassembly.

results.result: Endogenous ESCRT-III filaments stabilized by Vps4 depletion form uniform membrane-deforming conical spirals approximately 108 nm in diameter with ~4 turns, containing heteropolymers of multiple ESCRT-III proteins including CHMP6, CHMP2B, and CHMP1B. Filaments range from 4-15 nm in width and spiral in both left- and right-handed directions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C26-C34, and C70-C74 are well-supported by deep-etch EM observations (Figures 2 and 3) and immunogold labeling data (Figure 2B). Quantitative measurements of spiral diameter, filament width, and spiral handedness are provided with appropriate sample sizes. The structural characterization is comprehensive and represents a major advance in visualizing endogenous ESCRT-III assemblies.

results.result: CHMP4A alone forms flat filament networks that do not deform membranes, but coexpression of CHMP4A with CHMP2A (with at least one protein in an 'open' conformation) produces membrane-deforming spiral filaments. This membrane deformation does not depend on C-terminal autoinhibitory sequences in either protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 and C77-C82 are supported by deep-etch EM observations of transfected cells (Figure 4). The data demonstrate that heteropolymer formation is required for membrane deformation, as neither CHMP4A nor CHMP2A alone produces conical spirals. The experiments with truncated and full-length proteins provide evidence that autoinhibitory domains are not required for the membrane-deforming activity once heteropolymers form.

results.result: In cells depleted of Vps4, HIV-1 Gag assemblies on the plasma membrane are surrounded by single ESCRT-III filaments (4.5-12.8 nm wide) that are connected to Gag by perpendicular struts (~14 nm long). In control cells with normal Vps4 levels, ESCRT-III is not detected around Gag assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C40-C47, C90, and C91 are supported by deep-etch EM observations (Figures 5 and 6) and immunogold labeling (Figure 6D). The data show that Vps4 depletion traps ESCRT-III filaments around nascent Gag assemblies, while ESCRT-III is only transiently present in control cells. The structural observations of encircling filaments and connecting struts are well-documented with quantitative measurements.

results.result: The p6 domain of Gag, which contains PTAP and LYPXnL motifs for ESCRT-I and ALIX binding, is required for both VLP release and ESCRT-III recruitment. Deletion of p6 results in arrested Gag-containing buds without surrounding ESCRT-III rings.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 are supported by deep-etch EM observations of GagΔp6-expressing cells (Figure 7). The data demonstrate that p6 deletion prevents both VLP release and ESCRT-III recruitment, regardless of Vps4 status. The PTAP and LYPXnL motifs are well-established in the literature (C48-C50), and the experimental data confirm their functional importance.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which Vps4 has a previously unappreciated role in separating ESCRT-III from cargo (such as Gag) to allow centripetal growth of a neck-constricting ESCRT-III spiral. In this model, ESCRT-III first encircles cargo, then Vps4 releases connections between ESCRT-III and cargo, allowing the spiral to grow and drive membrane scission.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C54-C57, C62, and C63 represent a proposed mechanistic model based on interpolation between observed structures. While the model is consistent with the structural observations (encircled Gag assemblies in Vps4-depleted cells and completed spirals), it remains speculative. The model makes testable predictions (C62-C63), but direct evidence for the proposed sequence of events and the specific role of Vps4 in cargo separation is lacking. Dynamic imaging or additional functional experiments would be needed to validate this model.

results.result: Interfering with Vps4 activity increases ESCRT-III recovered in released VLPs.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by experimental observations by the authors (mentioned as 'data not shown') and by cited research (Van Engelenburg et al., 2014). While the authors' own data are not shown, the claim is corroborated by independent published work, providing reasonable support for this prediction of their model.

results.result: ESCRT-III spirals (~110 nm outer diameter in mammalian cells) correspond in size to the membrane area needed to generate vesicles of ~50 nm diameter, matching the typical size of ILVs in mammalian cells. This is analogous to in vitro observations where ESCRT-II with ESCRT-III proteins generated rings appropriate for yeast ILV sizes (25-35 nm).
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C95-C98 are supported by measurements from deep-etch EM (C31) and comparison to established ILV sizes from the literature (C97-C98). The correlation between spiral size and vesicle size is reasonable, though the inference that spirals define vesicle content (C31) remains speculative. The comparison to prior in vitro work (C95-C96) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: Background information on ESCRT machinery: ESCRT proteins and Vps4 drive membrane scission in multiple cellular processes; there are 7 ESCRT-III proteins in yeast and 12 in humans; ESCRT-III proteins cycle between inactive and active states; specific ESCRT-III proteins have distinct roles in nucleation, cargo confinement, polymer capping, and Vps4 recruitment; Vps4 remodels and disassembles ESCRT-III polymers.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C8-C23, and C100-C107 represent established knowledge in the ESCRT field, supported by extensive citations to prior research. These claims provide necessary background context but do not represent new findings from this study.

results.result: Background information on HIV-1 budding and ESCRT dynamics: Gag polymerization drives HIV-1 assembly and recruits ESCRT proteins; ESCRT-III and Vps4 are transiently recruited to budding sites; Vps4 is recruited before viral particle release and appears at multiple stages in cellular processes; ESCRT-III and Vps4 are present for only a few minutes at their sites of action.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C61, C66-C67, and C83-C91 represent established knowledge about HIV-1 budding and ESCRT dynamics, supported by citations to prior research. These claims provide context for the experimental observations but do not represent new findings.

results.result: Speculative interpretations: ESCRT-III puncta on plasma membranes could reflect roles in ectosome formation or MVB exocytosis; the observed struts connecting ESCRT-III to Gag could correspond to Alix, ESCRT-I, or ESCRT-I-ESCRT-II supercomplexes based on size.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C69 and C92-C94 represent speculative interpretations of observed structures. While the speculations are reasonable and supported by citations to relevant literature, they lack direct experimental evidence. The identity of the struts (C92-C94) remains uncertain because available antibodies were unsuitable for immunodecoration.

results.result: Methodological observations: Overexpressed FLAG-tagged CHMP4 proteins create flat filament networks; deep-etch EM is well-suited for examining plasma membrane morphology; ESCRT-III puncta in Vps4-depleted cells appear on both endosome-like structures and at the cell edge associated with unroofed plasma membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35, C108-C110 describe methodological observations and technical considerations. C35 is supported by prior work from the authors; C108 is supported by citation to methodological literature; C109-C110 are supported by observations in Figure 1A. These are valid but represent minor technical points.
